# 20-2-2025

## Intestinal transporters / EHC

There's conflicting information regarding the extend at which PFAS are excreted via the bile, undergo enterohepatic circulation or active transport in the intestine/liver. Recently a study on different intestinal models, fully characterised on their transporter protein expression, determined the apparent permeability of different PFASs among which PFOA and concluded that no active transport seemed to play a significant role in their transport.

# 19-2-2025

## Enterohepatic circulation

Binding affinities of PFAS to ASBT and NTCP seem to determine the freabs of PFAS through enterohepatic circulation. PFAS can mimic endogenous ligand TCE to bind to the active pockets of the proteins.

Physiologically, approximately 5% of the bile acids content normally escapes from reabsorption per cycle [@cao2022] .

![RF scores for the binding of PFAS to rat ASBT and NTCP. Max freab was set to 0.95 for TCA. from Cao et al. 2022](images/clipboard-2097976571.png)

# 18-2-2025

## Fecal clearance

Initial fecal clearance was 0.004 L/d [@fujii2015]

Changing it to 0 didn't change anything:

```         
print(AUC) [1] 170.6439 >   print(HalfLife) [1] 3.345812
```

*(initial model predictions:* AUC of **170.05** and a half life of **3.25** years)

Changing to kco, that being the colonic transit time overestimates the elimination:

## ![](images/clipboard-3688813787.png){width="276"}

## Kidney

I started with the most complex version of the kidney. That being:

-   Proximal tubule Plasma - Cell - Lumen
    -   active secretion between plasma and cell
    -   active reabsorption from lumen to cell
    -   passive permeability between plasma/cell/lumen
-   Rest of kidney Plasma - Lumen

The AUC was at **29.75072** ug.day/L and the half life at **3.51** years. Most of PFOA stays in the proximal tubule cell as passive permeability back to the plasma is very slow compared to the active secretion.

![](images/clipboard-3319694067.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-2695888055.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-2278906151.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-502054234.png){width="312"}

The distribution of PFOA in kidney tissue has not been explored and there's no indication of PFOA accumulation in kidney cells in literature. The predicted AUC seems to be quite low compared to the experimental one, therefore one could assume that either the active secretion from the plasma to the tissue is overestimated or that the passive permeability underestimated. I therefore tried to test a decreased active secretion by a factor 1e6. It did increase the AUC but still most of PFOA stays in the proximal tubule cells

![](images/clipboard-941815624.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-3063472549.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-1513618346.png){width="312"}

I also tried increasing the passive permeability by a factor of 10 and that increased the AUC to **95** ug.day/L and decreased the half life to **2.02** years.

![](images/clipboard-1450947478.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-3818905646.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-1687259873.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-685849692.png){width="312"}

The above simulation is quite close to the experimental data, however given the low confidence in all the above mentioned mechanisms, another approach could be to simplify the model and decrease the uncertainties. One could also re-compartmentalise the model when more data regarding the exact mechanisms involved in the distribution of PFOA between kidney plasma and kidney tissue are available.

Therefore the kidney was simplified to:

-   Proximal tubule tissue - Lumen

    -   active reabsorption from lumen to tissue
    -   passive permeability between tissue/lumen

-   Rest of kidney tissue - Lumen

With this approach the kidney model describes the mechanisms for which we are most confident about (i.e reabsorption from filtrate back to the proximal tubule). The predictions were an AUC of **170.05** and a half life of **3.25** years.

![](images/clipboard-2948566541.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-1282975824.png){width="312"}

One could also simplify the kidney even more by only dividing it to kidney tissue and kidney filtrate (lumen). However this is overestimating the re-absorption, as it assumes no flow out of the proximal tubule lumen other than the daily urinary excretion flow (1ml/min). This indeed predicts an AUC of **193.20** and a half life of **53.91.** In reality tubular fluid flow is important is an important aspect of kidney physiology. It's regulated based on the GFR and urinary pH. The tubular flow at the end of the proximal tubule is at 43.2 ml/min.

![](images/clipboard-2281072355.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-4079678327.png){width="312"}

So the best approach to modelling the kidney, based on the currently available *in vitro* and physiological data is:

-   Proximal tubule tissue - Lumen

    -   active reabsorption from lumen to tissue
    -   passive permeability between tissue/lumen

-   Rest of kidney tissue - Lumen

Active reabsorption clearance was transformed to Vmax/Km to account for transporter saturation. The updated AUC was at **169** and half life at **3.24** years.

![](images/clipboard-2124753294.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-1314773932.png){width="312"}

Regarding the first part of the kinetics, predicted absorption to the plasma is much quicker in the model.

![](images/clipboard-3808099951.png){width="312"}

# 16-2-2025

I looked into the complex kidney model. The half-life in the complex model is at **1.79** years, while the AUC is at **43.98**. So half-life is closer to the realistic ones, but AUC is low.

Having a SF = 1 is decreasing the half-life to 0.16 years but is not changing the AUC. So basically this is reducing the re-absorption, but everything was already eliminated the AUC stayed low.

One could think that the AUC is low because of the fast GFR. So I tested decreasing the fraction unbound by a factor of 10 and that decreased both the AUC and t1/2.

![](images/clipboard-3903282594.png){width="312"}

Changing the active clearances to Km/Vmax increased the half-life to **2.02** years and decreased the AUC to **28.31**. So basically here due to saturation of the re-absorption, the half-life increased, but elimination was never saturated so elimination kept decreasing the concentration from plasma.

![](images/clipboard-4280058655.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-3422009043.png){width="312"}

I then tried to merge the compartments to have a kidney plasma, kidney cell and kidney filtrate compartment and that caused a t1/2 of **72.27** years and an AUC of **34.56**. So compared to the complex model now the half life is increased. I think here is a competition between the active clearances. The concentration both in the filtrate and the kidney plasma is diluted, but not the one in the cell. !! This I don't understand might need to re-do!

Then going back to a Proximal Tubule and Rest of Kidney but a common filtrate compartment caused a t1/2 of **81.86** and an AUC of **51.16**. Both the AUC t1/2 and AUC here increased. So it seems like isolating the filtrate to the proximal compartment and accounting for the flow of urine out of the proximal compartment is important. Because if we keep a common filtrate compartment then the re-absorption is higher because everything just stagnates there. Active re-absorption only happens in the proximal tubule so that should be accounted for.

I also tried merging Proximal Tubule Plasma with Proximal Tubule Cells. Then the t1.2 decreased to 0.82 and the AUC increased to 101.47. So it seems like indeed more is going back to the blood, but then more is cleared out, without it getting enough re-absorbed. Adding or removing active/passive processes didn't change anything regarding the half life (nor the AUC actually).

Going back to the simple kidney, GFR should be leaving from plasma and not from the kidney:

**If SF = 1** then all is good: AUC = 186.93 and t1/2 = 3.9 years.

![](images/clipboard-5311209.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-3008961444.png){width="312"}

With normal SF, then AUC = 205.68 and t1/2 = 26.22 years.

![](images/clipboard-3869192757.png){width="312"}

As all the active processes happen in the proximal tubule I think it's important that we separate that compartment from the rest of the kidney. So as a first step I separated the proximal tubule lumen (primary filtrate) from the rest of the urine. Primary urine flow to the rest of the proximal tubule lumen was taken from literature (Scotcher et al.. Pletz et al., MechKin etc). With this update, **AUC is now at 159.98** and t1/2 is at **1.55 years**, so both are within the bulk.

![](images/clipboard-51335127.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-1739236625.png){width="312"}

One could also consider simplifying, by only accounting for active reabsorption, as this is the major mechanism involved in PFAS excretion. This results in an **AUC of 162.0108 and a t1/2 of 1.63.**

![](images/clipboard-2647008661.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-1907083448.png){width="312"}

But given the results shown in @fig-RenalClearance at least active secretion shouldn't be ignored.

If active processes are involved but passive processes not, then **AUC is at 157.64 and t1/2 is at 1.46**. Literature studies showed that PFASs and especially PFOA has been associated with chronic kidney disease and a decreased GFR. Patients with chronic kidney disease have also lower urine and kidney tubule pH which could lead to an increased fraction un-ionised of PFOA and therefore higher passive reabsorption from the tubule. This mechanism would be relevant for predicting PFAS concentrations for this population.

::: callout-important
## Separating proximal tubule lumen to rest of kidney lumen gives better predictions, without needing to fit the SF.
:::

When rest of the kidney tissue was also separated then the AUC stayed approx the same, at 126, but the t1/2 decreased to 0.79 years. I think this is because the concentration in the kidney proximal tissue is increased so the active secretion there is more important. Actually thinking now I think only active reabsorption and passive permeability on the side of the filtrate should matter because we can't really validate what happens on the apical side.

![](images/clipboard-853479559.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-1919616793.png){width="312"}

Indeed, when I remove the active secretion, then the half life is back to 1.71 years and the AUC is at 161.98

![](images/clipboard-3583364250.png){width="312"} ![](images/clipboard-2081811787.png){width="312"}

::: callout-important
Indeed separating proximal tubule tissue/plasma and lumen and rest of kidney tissue/plasma and lumen with active and passive clearances on the luminal side seems the most accurate way of doing a mechanistic kidney without increasing the uncertainties.
:::

Even if we choose to go with a mix kidney tissue/plasma and proximal tubule filtrate + rest of kidney filtrate without active secretion from the plasma then AUC is at 164 and t1/2 is at 1.73

```{r}
#| label: fig-LocalSAonSF
#| eval: false
#| fig-cap: Sensitivity of Scaling Factor on Renal Clearance Parameters
#| include: false
#| layout-ncol: 2


CalcClearances <- function(SF){
  
  MW <- 414.1
  pKa <- 1.886 # average of all the experimental values
  GFR <- 175.6888
  fVPTC <- 0.511
  VPT <- 0.1115421
  fup <- 0.061/100
  
  # Input Renal Clearance Data ####
  
  CL_OAT1 = 19*60*24  # Clearance L/d/mg protein (scaled from uL/min/mg protein)
  Vmax_OAT1 = 3.5*MW*1e-3*60*24 # ug/d/mg protein (nmol -> ug, min -> d) (scaled from nmol/min/mg protein)
  Km_OAT1 = 185*MW # ug/L (scaled from uM)
  
  CL_OAT3 = 17*60*24  # Clearance L/d/mg protein (scaled from uL/min/mg protein)
  Vmax_OAT3 = 1.5*MW*1e-3*60*24 # ug/d/mg protein (nmol -> ug, min -> d) (scaled from nmol/min/mg protein)
  Km_OAT3 = 90*MW # ug/L (scaled from uM)
  
  CL_OAT4 = 96*60*24  # Clearance L/d/mg protein (scaled from uL/min/mg protein)
  Vmax_OAT4 = 4.5*MW*1e-3*60*24 # ug/d/mg protein (nmol -> ug, min -> d) (scaled from nmol/min/mg protein)
  Km_OAT4 = 47*MW # ug/L (scaled from uM)
  
  Papp = 1.46*1e-6 # cm/d (scaled from *10e-6 cm/sec)
  
  
  # Scaling Renal Clearance Data ####
  
  # Scaling Factor
  # SF <- 10.9e-6 * 99.4e6 * 1e3*REF #6.54 mgprotein/HEK293cell (ref: Han and Ni, 2004; Ho et al., 2004) * PTCPGK cells/g kidney * 1e3 as Vkidney is in Kg (could be 99.4e6 or 60e6 see below comment ref: Neuhoff et al., 2013), equation from: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.comtox.2021.100172 
  # Comment regarding PTCPGK: from Tang et al. 2024 https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.molpharmaceut.4c00504  a value of 60 million PTCPGKis commonly used but the observed value as high as 209 million PTCPGK has been reported. In this study, avalue of 99.4 million PTCPGK was applied based on the mostrecent meta-analysis.45 
  # SF <- 0.17 * 10e6 # 17% of kidney is protein [ICRP 89], 10e6 is scaling from mg protein to kg protein, double ref for 17% protein Ruark 2020: DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-818596-4.00006-0
  # These scaling factors are not too far off. Scaling based on protein gives 1.7e6, scaling for cells gives 1.08346e6
  
  ## Active ####
  # Secretion
  CL_PltPT <- (CL_OAT1 + CL_OAT3) * SF * (fVPTC*VPT) #L/d, corrected to proximal tubule volume only
  
  # Re-absorption
  CL_FiltPT <- CL_OAT4 * SF * (fVPTC*VPT) # L/d, corrected to proximal tubule volume only
  
 
  ## Fraction un-bound ####
  
  # To calculate fraction unbound in tissue based on the Poulin and Theil equation
  # R is the ratio of average albumin and lipoprotein in tissue / plasma
  
  # Albumin concentrations
  # From Akihiro Tojo and Satoshi Kinugasa 2012 doi:10.1155/2012/481520
  # Calb_GlomL <- 22.9 #ug/ml bowmans capsule
  # Calb_PT <- 14.4 #ug/ml proximal tubule 
  # Calb_DT <- 1.3 #ug/ml distal tubule
  # Calb_Ur <- 0.7 #ug/ml urine
  # In the same paper: the proximal tubule reabsorbes 71% of albumin, while LoH and DT 23% and the collecting duct 3%
  Calb_P <- 37.0      #mg/ml plasma
  Calb_L <- 0.00864   #mg/ml filtrate (kidney lumen)
 
  # Albumin ratio
  R_T <- 0.5 #albumin and lipoprotein ratio between the tissue interstitial fluid and plasma
  R_Fil <- Calb_L/Calb_P  # or 0.00062

  
  # Fraction unbound
  fuT <- 1/(1 + ((1 - fup)/fup) * R_T)     # Poulin and Theil, 2009, below Table 6
  fuFil <- 1/(1 + ((1 - fup)/fup) * R_Fil)
 
  CL_secr <- CL_PltPT
  CL_reab <- CL_FiltPT
  
  return(c(CL_secr, CL_reab))
}


SensiSF <- function(){
  
  SF_values <- 10^(seq(-10, 10, by=2))
  
  Sensitivity_results <- matrix(nrow = length(SF_values), ncol=2)
  Changed_clearances <- matrix(nrow = length(SF_values), ncol=2)
  Original_clearances <- CalcClearances(1083460)
  
  for(i in 1:length(SF_values)){
    
    Changed_clearances[i,] <- CalcClearances(SF_values[i])
    Sensitivity_results[i, ] <- (abs(Changed_clearances[i,] -
                                       Original_clearances)/Original_clearances)/
      (abs(SF_values[i]-1)/1)
  }

  return(Sensitivity_results)

}

SA_results <- as.data.frame(SensiSF())
colnames(SA_results) <- c("CL_secr", "CL_reab")

SA_df <- SA_results %>% mutate(SF = c(10^(seq(-10, 10, by=2)))) %>% 
  pivot_longer(names_to = "Clearance", values_to = "SI", CL_secr:CL_reab)
SA_df$Clearance <- as.factor(SA_df$Clearance) 

ggplot(SA_df, aes(x = log10(SF), y = SI, fill = Clearance)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey", "grey49"))+
  ylab("Sensitivity index")+
  xlab("Scaling factor (log10())") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1)

```
